title: Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 24 Sep 2026]
    Title:Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A skill is a modular package of natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and reference resources that an agent can load at runtime to extend its capabilities for a specific task. Skill-based agent systems therefore enable flexible reuse of third-party capabilities, but the openness of this skill ecosystem also opens up a new attack surface. Prior work has focused on vulnerabilities within individual skills, but little attention has been paid to risks that arise from interactions across skills. In this paper, we introduce skill cascading attacks, a threat paradigm in which a malicious objective is distributed across multiple skills so that each modification looks benign in isolation, yet their combined execution is harmful. For instance, in a prescription-review pipeline, the first skill weakens signals of recently discontinued medications in the extracted history, the second downgrades the severity of any drug interaction tied to them, and the third suppresses the resulting low-priority alert in the final summary, so that a severe drug-interaction warning silently disappears before reaching the physician. To systematically study this safety blind spot, we develop SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and release SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains. Across representative agents (e.g., OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and LLM backbones, cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors. Our findings highlight a gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety, and call for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than individual skills in isolation.

report.summary: A new paper introduces skill cascading attacks, where individually benign skills combine to trigger harmful agent behavior, and releases SkillCascade-Bench to test defenses.
report.background: Skill-based agent systems let agents load third-party modular skills—natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference resources—at runtime. This openness enables flexible reuse of capabilities, but it also creates a broad attack surface. Prior security research has mostly examined vulnerabilities inside individual skills, such as prompt injection, malicious code, or unsafe content. However, real agent workflows often chain multiple skills into pipelines, where small benign-looking edits can interact. The paper argues that this cross-skill interaction is a safety blind spot. For example, in a prescription-review pipeline, separate skills can weaken medication-history signals, downgrade drug-interaction severity, and suppress an alert. Together they remove a severe warning, even though each skill passes per-skill review. The authors propose skill cascading attacks and build an automated red-teaming framework to systematically expose this emerging risk.
key_points: Skill cascading attacks distribute a malicious objective across multiple skills. Each skill appears benign in isolation, but their combined execution causes harm. In a prescription-review example, one skill weakens discontinued-medication signals, another downgrades drug-interaction severity, and a third suppresses the final low-priority alert, silently removing a severe warning before it reaches a physician.

The researchers introduce SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and release SkillCascade-Bench. The benchmark contains 213 validated cascading test cases spanning multiple agent systems and domains. It is designed to systematically study how cross-skill interactions can induce harmful behavior while avoiding detection by conventional per-skill security checks.

Evaluations across representative agents such as OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex, plus different LLM backbones, show cascaded interactions reliably trigger harmful behaviors. The attacks evade existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors. This demonstrates that component-level integrity does not guarantee system-level safety in open skill ecosystems.

The findings highlight a defense gap: current security tools inspect skills one at a time, but harm emerges from their composition. Effective defenses must reason over cross-skill interactions, tracking data flow, intent, and policy violations across the full pipeline rather than trusting each skill independently.

The work matters for agent platforms, skill marketplaces, and enterprise deployments. It suggests that skill versioning, provenance, composition analysis, and runtime monitoring of inter-skill dependencies should become standard safeguards as third-party skills proliferate.

The paper calls for defenses that model the whole skill graph. Potential directions include taint tracking across skill boundaries, policy engines for multi-step workflows, and red-team benchmarks that test realistic agent pipelines in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and security operations.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this research shifts attention from individual skill safety to system-level safety in agent ecosystems. Skill marketplaces and agent platforms may need composition-aware vetting, provenance tracking, and policy enforcement before third-party skills are combined. Security vendors will likely add cross-skill taint analysis, runtime intent monitoring, and red-teaming services. Developers must treat skill graphs as attack surfaces, test multi-skill pipelines, pin versions, and monitor emergent behavior. Regular users could face silent failures in high-stakes workflows, such as health, finance, or compliance, where agents assemble third-party capabilities. The paper raises trust and regulatory questions for autonomous agents and shows that current guardrails are insufficient against coordinated, distributed attacks.
report.tools: Watch SkillCascade and SkillCascade-Bench for red-teaming skill pipelines. Agent runtimes such as OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex are useful for reproducing the evaluation. Complementary open-source projects include PyRIT and Garak for adversarial testing, NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails and Guardrails AI for runtime policies, LangSmith or LangFuse for tracing cross-skill calls, and AgentDojo for broader agent security benchmarking.
